notes.meaning: Jesus knows what His neighbors are thinking. They have heard about the miracles He performed in Capernaum, and their pride makes them feel entitled to see the same wonders in Nazareth. Jesus uses a well-known proverb to show that their demand comes from doubt and a desire for proof, not from real faith.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think Luke moved this Nazareth visit earlier in his Gospel to show the typical pattern of Jesus' ministry, since Luke has not yet recorded the Capernaum miracles mentioned here.

notes.meaning: Jesus explains why He will not put on a display of power for them. People who watched Him grow up think they know Him too well to respect Him as a messenger from God. Their familiarity with Him makes them blind to who He really is.

Jesus reminds them of the great drought in Elijah's day, when no rain fell for three and a half years and food was scarce. Even though there were many needy widows in Israel, God did not send Elijah to help any of them. Instead, God sent His prophet to care for a foreign widow in Sidon, showing that God gives His gifts according to His own wisdom rather than national privilege.

Jesus gives a second example from the days of Elisha. There were many Israelites who suffered from leprosy, a painful skin disease, but none of them was cured. The only person healed was Naaman, a military leader from the enemy land of Syria, because God chose to show mercy to an outsider who came in faith.

The people in the synagogue became furious when they understood what Jesus meant. He was telling them that God had bypassed Israel before to bless foreigners, and that their own unbelief was cutting them off from His grace. Their hurt pride quickly turned their earlier admiration into deep hatred.

The crowd turned into a mob, grabbed Jesus, and forced Him out of their town. They dragged Him to the edge of the hill on which Nazareth stood, intending to throw Him over the cliff to kill Him. Their violent reaction showed how far human anger can go when people refuse to hear the truth about themselves.

Jesus walked calmly right through the middle of the hostile mob and went on His way. God preserved His Son because it was not yet His time to die. No enemy could take His life until His work was fully completed.

differ.view: Jesus was rescued by a miracle of divine power, as God restrained the mob by blinding their eyes, holding their hands, or stunning their minds.
Jesus may have been made invisible or so overawed the crowd by His divine presence that they lost all power to lay hands on Him.
No supernatural miracle was needed, because the calm moral majesty of a holy person can naturally disarm an angry mob.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Jesus performed a clear miracle that showed His divinity by making His attackers powerless to touch Him.

notes.meaning: After leaving Nazareth, Jesus traveled down to Capernaum, a town beside the Sea of Galilee. He made this city His new base of ministry. On the Sabbath, the Jewish day of rest and worship, He regularly taught the people in their synagogue.

The people were astonished by what they heard. Unlike their usual religious teachers who merely repeated the words of older rabbis, Jesus spoke with direct divine authority. His words carried a commanding power that went straight to their consciences.
While Jesus was teaching in the synagogue, a man possessed by an evil spirit began shouting. Even in a place set apart for worship, the demonic spirit could not remain quiet in the presence of Jesus.

The demon cried out in terror, asking if Jesus had come to destroy evil spirits. It publicly declared that Jesus was the Holy One sent from God. The demons recognized who Jesus was even while most people still doubted Him.

Jesus sternly commanded the demon to be silent and ordered it to leave the man. The evil spirit threw the man down violently in front of everyone, but Jesus' power protected the man so that he was not harmed at all.

The whole congregation was filled with wonder at what they had witnessed. Other healers used long rituals or spells, but Jesus simply gave a command, and the unclean spirits had to obey. They recognized that His message carried unmatched heavenly power.
Reports about what Jesus had done spread quickly throughout the entire region. People everywhere began sharing the news of His powerful teaching and miracles.

Jesus left the synagogue and went home with Simon Peter. Peter's mother-in-law was terribly ill with a severe, dangerous fever. The family immediately asked Jesus to help her, trusting that He had the power to heal.

Jesus stood over the sick woman and rebuked the fever, ordering it to leave her. Her health returned at once, without any lingering weakness, and she immediately got up to prepare food and serve her guests. When the Lord restores us, our renewed strength should be gladly used to serve Him and others.

As the sun set, the Sabbath officially ended, and people were free to carry their sick through the streets. A large crowd brought men and women suffering from all kinds of illnesses to Jesus. He cared for each one personally, placing His hands on them and healing them all.

Demons also came out of many people, shouting that Jesus was the Son of God. Jesus silenced them and would not allow them to speak, because He refused to accept testimony from the devil. He did not want anyone to think He was in partnership with evil spirits.

At daybreak, Jesus went out to a lonely, quiet place to pray by Himself. The crowds searched until they found Him and begged Him not to leave their town. Even though their desire to keep Him was strong, Jesus could not let popularity distract Him from His true mission.

Jesus told the people that He had to preach the good news about God's kingdom to other towns as well. He could not stay in one comfortable place, because spreading God's message was the very reason His Father had sent Him.
Jesus traveled throughout the region, preaching in the synagogues everywhere He went. He remained faithful to His calling, sharing the word of God with all who gathered to worship.
